name: Leuprolide (GnRH agonist puberty blocker)

card.summary: A prescription GnRH agonist that pauses puberty in medical settings; its use to extend growth in short-stature protocols is investigational and unproven.
card.note: Prescription-only hormone therapy with documented bone-density, metabolic and other adverse effects.

quick.overview:
Leuprolide is a synthetic version of gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH), the brain signal that starts puberty. Given continuously, it switches off the pituitary signal to the gonads, which lowers sex hormones. It is approved for prostate cancer, endometriosis, uterine fibroids and central precocious puberty.

In height-focused discussions it is mentioned as a way to delay puberty and growth plate closure in some short-stature protocols. That use is off-label, and the sources reviewed describe it as investigational; no trial has established that it raises adult height in otherwise healthy short children.
quick.mechanism: After an initial short-lived rise in luteinising and follicle-stimulating hormone, continuous exposure desensitises GnRH receptors on the pituitary, so testosterone and estrogen fall to very low levels. The effect is reversible after stopping. Because estrogen drives growth plate maturation, suppressing it slows skeletal maturation.
quick.risks: The US label for leuprolide products lists a transient testosterone flare, hyperglycemia and diabetes, cardiovascular disease, QT prolongation, convulsions and severe skin reactions among warnings, and reports hot flashes and fatigue as common. Bone mineral density loss is documented with prolonged therapy. It is prescription-only and may cause fetal harm.

lead: Leuprolide (leuprorelin) is a synthetic gonadotropin-releasing hormone (GnRH) agonist, administered by injection, that lowers testosterone and estradiol by desensitising pituitary GnRH receptors [1][2]. It was patented in 1973 and introduced for medical use in 1985 [1]. It is approved for advanced prostate cancer, and elsewhere for endometriosis, fibroids and central precocious puberty [1][3].

In looksmaxxing and height discussions, it is sometimes described as a puberty blocker that might delay growth plate fusion and thereby extend the window for growth. Published sources describe puberty suppression in central precocious puberty, where treatment slows bone age advancement [4], but they describe use for ordinary short stature as investigational and unproven [4].
Leuprolide is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the EU and Australia [1]. Its US labelling documents tumour flare, hyperglycemia, cardiovascular risk and other warnings [3].
infobox: Prostate cancer, endometriosis, fibroids, central precocious puberty [1][3]

paras: Wikipedia lists hormone-responsive cancers such as prostate and breast cancer, endometriosis and uterine fibroids, central precocious puberty, ovarian protection during chemotherapy, and use in assisted reproduction as established or recognised uses, and also notes use to delay puberty in transgender youth [1]. The US label for a subcutaneous leuprolide product is indicated for advanced prostate cancer [3]. Fensolvi, a pediatric formulation, was approved for central precocious puberty in 2020 [1].

In central precocious puberty, GnRH agonists suppress early sex hormone release and slow puberty until a more typical age [5]. Registered trials include studies of leuprorelin depot formulations in children with central precocious puberty [6][7].

sections.h: Use in height and growth contexts
paras: Estrogen, in both sexes, accelerates growth plate maturation and eventually closure of the plates [8]. Because leuprolide lowers sex steroids, some height-focused discussions treat it as a way to hold the plates open longer. Grokipedia reports that in central precocious puberty it slows bone age advancement and is associated with improved predicted adult height compared with untreated cohorts, while describing use for short stature outside that condition as unproven without phase III confirmation [4].
No trial in the sources reviewed tests leuprolide to increase adult height in children without precocious puberty.

The label states that leuprolide acetate acts as an inhibitor of gonadotropin secretion when given continuously, after an initial stimulation, leading to suppression of testicular and ovarian steroid production, an effect that is reversible after stopping treatment [3]. In men a temporary testosterone rise of about 50 percent can occur in the first one to two weeks [1]. A general description of GnRH agonists puts testosterone at 140 to 200 percent of baseline early on, falling to castrate levels within two to four weeks [5].

The US label lists tumour flare, hyperglycemia and diabetes, cardiovascular disease, QT/QTc prolongation, convulsions and severe cutaneous adverse reactions among its warnings; the most common reactions include malaise, fatigue and hot flashes or sweats [3]. Wikipedia adds injection-site reactions, headache, reduced sexual interest, gynecomastia in roughly 3 to 16 percent, and notes that label updates between 2010 and 2013 added loss of bone density, thromboembolism and convulsions [1].

A 40-man study of leuprolide for prostate cancer reported changes in body composition during androgen deprivation [9], and a randomised trial examined pamidronate to prevent bone loss during androgen deprivation therapy [10]. Wikipedia reports that a cohort of women treated for precocious puberty as children reported osteoporosis and brittle teeth, though the FDA has not established causation [1]. The label states that leuprolide may cause fetal harm in pregnancy [3].

Leuprolide is prescription-only in the US, Canada, the EU and Australia and is on the WHO Model List of Essential Medicines [1]. In 2001, TAP Pharmaceuticals paid $875 million to settle federal and state charges of fraud and illegal marketing relating to leuprorelin [1].

No studies found testing leuprolide for height gain in children or adults with normal-variant short stature. Human trials of leuprolide exist for other conditions: a randomised trial of leuprolide with or without flutamide in prostate cancer [11], a comparison with diethylstilbestrol [12], and registered phase 4 trials in central precocious puberty [6][7].
